newsitem.title: UK: Iran/Turkmen gas line not seen affecting Europe.
newsitem.headline: Iran/Turkmen gas line not seen affecting Europe.

text.p: Washington's decision not to oppose on legal grounds a proposed pipeline bringing gas from Turkmenistan to Europe across Iran is highly unlikely to have any impact on supplies to Europe, a leading analyst said on Monday.

Jonathan Stern, senior Vice President of consultants Gas Strategies, said that even if the line goes ahead, it would only deliver gas as far as southeastern Turkey and would not compete with any existing gas supplies.
A spokeswoman for President Clinton said on Sunday that the administration has determined that the 1996 Iran-Libya Sanctions Act (ILSA) does not apply to the pipeline.
The first leg of the project, a line taking Turkmen gas into north eastern Iran, is expected to be completed this winter.

But Stern was dismissive of the impact on European supply. "This is gas with no other market," he said. "The only moment when it has a bearing is when it arrives in western or central Turkey, when it might compete with other supply."
But even then, he added, the gas with which it might compete was Russian gas piped across the Black Sea or coming through Caucasian republics, and these projects were still at the discussion stage.

The link to be completed this winter will only supply parts of Iran with Turkmen gas. "This connection is for Iranian consumption," he said. "The gas hasn't even reached anything that could be regarded as a gas market."

And he was sceptical about the possibility of a link eventually extending as far as Europe. "To my certain knowledge there have been discussions for 10 years about supplying Turkey from Iran," he said, adding that none have yet materialised.
The National Iranian Gas Company (NIGC) said in February that an Iran-Turkey pipeline carrying 3-10 billion cubic metres a year (bcm/y) was estimated to start in 1999 at a cost of $1.62 billion.
But the more ambitious Iran-Europe pipeline, carrying 8-32 bcm/y at a cost of $11 billion, was not expected to start until 2005, it said.
